claims.text: The initial material is a W–Cu composite containing tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten ligaments in a copper matrix.
The untreated composite lacks an additional interface-stabilizing dispersion.
TiC nanoparticles can be uniformly dispersed in the tungsten matrix during fabrication.
The proposed service conditions include high-temperature thermal cycling representative of W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
The proposed service conditions include irradiation representative of W-based plasma-facing material/Cu-based cooling-component joints.
The intervention will produce evenly distributed TiC nanoparticles at W–Cu interfaces.
TiC nanoparticles at W–Cu interfaces act as diffusion barriers.
The TiC diffusion barriers inhibit atomic interdiffusion between tungsten and copper.
Inhibiting W–Cu interdiffusion minimizes phase separation.
TiC interface stabilization prevents interfacial void formation.
Interface stabilization maintains thermal-conduction paths despite thermal- or irradiation-induced stresses.
The TiC-dispersed W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an untreated W–Cu composite under identical conditions.
The TiC-dispersed composite will exhibit less phase separation than the untreated composite.
The TiC-dispersed composite will exhibit fewer interfacial voids than the untreated composite.
The proposed effect is conditional on achieving a uniform TiC dispersion.
The proposed effect is limited to service environments typical of plasma-facing component joints.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity improvement remains unknown.
Potential trade-offs involving mechanical properties remain unknown.
